title: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
abstract: The Okapi BM25 ranking function represents one of the most successful and robust probabilistic retrieval models in Information Retrieval. Derived from the 2-Poisson model and probability ranking principle, BM25 scores documents based on term frequency saturation and document length normalization. This paper surveys the theoretical foundations of BM25, query term weights, and empirical parameter tuning.

title: A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing
abstract: In a vector space model, textual documents and queries are represented as vectors in a multi-dimensional space where each dimension corresponds to a distinct index term. The similarity between queries and stored documents is computed using the cosine of the angle between their vector representations, weighted by term frequency and inverse document frequency (TF-IDF).

title: A Language Modeling Approach to Information Retrieval
abstract: We present a statistical language modeling framework for text retrieval. Instead of computing relevance directly through ad-hoc term weights, each document is viewed as a statistical language model. Given a query, documents are ranked by the probability that the document model generated the query terms, employing Jelinek-Mercer and Dirichlet smoothing to handle unseen words.

title: Fast and Flexible Inverted Index Compression
abstract: Inverted indexes are the core data structure enabling fast full-text search across web-scale document collections. This paper investigates integer compression techniques for posting lists, including byte-aligned codes, Elias gamma/delta, and PForDelta. We analyze trade-offs between compression ratio and decompression throughput for ranked Boolean queries.

title: The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web
abstract: The importance of a Web page is an inherently subjective concept depending on the page's structural prominence and citation context. We introduce PageRank, a method for rating Web pages based on the graph topology of the hyperlink network. PageRank models an idealized random surfer traversing links with a damping factor, generating objective authority scores.

title: Evaluating Information Retrieval Systems: Measures and Methodology
abstract: Systematic evaluation of retrieval effectiveness is a cornerstone of Information Retrieval research. We analyze standardized evaluation measures including Precision at K, Recall at K, Mean Average Precision (MAP), and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG). We discuss statistical significance testing and relevance judgment pooling methodology.

title: Attention Is All You Need
abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. We propose the Transformer, a novel network architecture based entirely on self-attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. The Transformer achieves superior translation quality while being more parallelizable.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
abstract: We introduce BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers). Unlike recent language representation models, BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer for NLP tasks.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
abstract: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. We show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance. We train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, demonstrating remarkable zero-shot and few-shot capabilities.

title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
abstract: We propose two novel model architectures for computing continuous vector representations of words from vast datasets: the Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) and continuous Skip-gram models (Word2Vec). The models capture syntactic and semantic word relationships with high accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity compared to neural network language models.

title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
abstract: Recent methods for learning vector space representations of words succeed either at capturing global co-occurrence statistics or local context window properties. We construct GloVe, an unsupervised learning algorithm that combines the advantages of both: global matrix factorization and local context windows, minimizing a log-bilinear model over non-zero elements in a word co-occurrence matrix.

title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
abstract: Deeper neural networks are notoriously difficult to train due to vanishing and exploding gradients. We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs. Residual networks (ResNets) with up to 152 layers won ImageNet 2015.

title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: We trained a large, deep convolutional neural network (AlexNet) to classify the 1.2 million high-resolution images in the ImageNet LSVRC-2010 contest into 1000 different classes. The neural network consists of five convolutional layers, max-pooling, and three fully-connected layers with dropout regularization. This work catalyzed the deep learning revolution.

title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
abstract: Deep neural networks with a large number of parameters are very powerful machine learning systems, but overfitting is a serious problem. Dropout is a technique for addressing this problem. The key idea is to randomly drop units along with their connections from the neural network during training, preventing complex co-adaptations between features.

title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
abstract: We introduce Adam, an algorithm for first-order gradient-based optimization of stochastic objective functions, based on adaptive estimates of lower-order moments. The method is straightforward to implement, is computationally efficient, has little memory requirements, is invariant to diagonal rescaling of the gradients, and is well-suited for problems that are large in terms of data or parameters.

title: Generative Adversarial Nets
abstract: We propose a new framework for estimating generative models via an adversarial process, in which we simultaneously train two models: a generative model G that captures the data distribution, and a discriminative model D that estimates the probability that a sample came from the training data rather than G. The training procedure corresponds to a minimax two-player game.

title: Random Forests: Principles and Applications
abstract: Random forests are a combination of tree predictors such that each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest. The generalization error for forests converges to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large, offering strong resistance to overfitting and excellent classification accuracy.

title: Mining Association Rules between Sets of Items in Large Databases
abstract: We address the problem of discovering association rules between items in large databases of sales transactions. Given a set of transactions, where each transaction is a set of literals (items), we discover all rules that have support and confidence greater than user-specified minimum thresholds. We present the Apriori algorithm, which uses the downward-closure property of itemset support.

title: Fast Algorithms for Mining Association Rules in Large Databases
abstract: We present two new algorithms, Apriori and AprioriTid, for discovering all significant association rules between items in a transaction database. These algorithms decompose the mining task into frequent itemset generation followed by rule derivation. We evaluate execution times and scaling properties on synthetic and real-world supermarket transaction databases.

title: Mining Frequent Patterns without Candidate Generation: A Frequent-Pattern Tree Approach
abstract: Mining frequent patterns in transaction databases has been a fundamental problem in data mining. Most existing algorithms generate and test huge sets of candidate itemsets. We propose a novel data structure, the Frequent-Pattern tree (FP-tree), and an associated mining algorithm (FP-Growth) that compresses the database into a compact tree and mines patterns without candidate generation.

title: Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations
abstract: The K-means clustering algorithm is an iterative technique designed to partition a dataset into K non-overlapping clusters. Each observation belongs to the cluster with the nearest mean, serving as a prototype of the cluster. We formalize convergence criteria, objective function minimization of within-cluster sum of squares, and cluster center updates.

title: A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases with Noise
abstract: Clustering algorithms are attractive for data mining tasks involving spatial and numerical collections. Traditional partitioning methods like K-means struggle with clusters of arbitrary shapes and outliers. We present DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise), which relies on a density-based notion of clusters to discover arbitrarily shaped groups.

title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
abstract: MapReduce is a programming model and an associated implementation for processing and generating large datasets. Users specify a map function that processes a key/value pair to generate a set of intermediate key/value pairs, and a reduce function that merges all intermediate values associated with the same intermediate key. The system handles partitioning, scheduling, and fault tolerance.

title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
abstract: Spanner is Google's scalable, multi-version, globally-distributed, and synchronously-replicated database. It provides externally consistent distributed transactions at global scale using the TrueTime API, which exposes clock uncertainty bounds. Spanner supports non-blocking reads in the past, atomic schema changes, and consistency across worldwide datacenters.

title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm: Raft
abstract: Raft is a consensus algorithm for managing a replicated log. It produces a result equivalent to multi-Paxos, and it is as efficient as Paxos, but its structure is different from Paxos; this makes Raft much more understandable than Paxos and provides a better foundation for building practical systems. Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety.
